name: The Double-Slit Experiment
statement: Send particles one at a time through two slits and they still build an interference pattern, as if each passed through both.
statementAccent: as if each passed through both
meaning: The double-slit experiment is a demonstration in physics in which particles or waves are sent through a barrier with two narrow slits and form a pattern of alternating bright and dark bands, an interference pattern, on a screen behind. It began as an optics experiment associated with Thomas Young, who in his Bakerian Lectures around 1801 and 1803 argued for the wave nature of light by showing that light passing two closely spaced openings produces interference fringes, the hallmark of waves overlapping and reinforcing or cancelling. Its deeper fame comes from the quantum version, in which single particles, such as electrons or photons, are fired one at a time. Each particle strikes the screen as a single localized dot, seemingly like a particle, yet over many particles the accumulated dots build up the same interference pattern, as though each particle somehow passed through both slits and interfered with itself. Crucially, if a detector is placed to determine which slit each particle went through, the interference pattern disappears and the particles behave like ordinary particles. The double-slit experiment thus dramatizes wave-particle duality and the role of measurement, and Richard Feynman called it a phenomenon containing the only mystery at the heart of quantum mechanics.
mechanism: In the classic wave form, coherent light passing through two narrow, closely spaced slits spreads out from each slit and the two overlapping waves interfere: where crests meet crests the light is bright, and where crests meet troughs it cancels, producing evenly spaced fringes whose spacing depends on the wavelength and geometry. In the quantum form, the same pattern emerges even when particles are sent through one at a time, so no particle can be interfering with another. The behavior is described by a wavefunction, a probability amplitude that passes through both slits and interferes with itself; the square of its magnitude gives the probability of the particle landing at each point, and this probability distribution has the fringe pattern. Each individual particle nonetheless registers as a single dot, and the pattern appears only in the statistics of many. If an apparatus records which slit a particle traversed, obtaining which-path information, the particle becomes correlated, or entangled, with that detector, the interference is lost, and two particle-like bands appear instead. This reflects Bohr's principle of complementarity: the wave-like interference and the particle-like which-path knowledge are mutually exclusive, and which behavior appears depends on what the apparatus is set up to detect.

examples.text: Thomas Young showed around 1801 to 1803 that light through two close openings makes interference fringes, evidence for the wave nature of light.
Firing electrons singly, each lands as one dot, yet the accumulated dots build up an interference pattern, as Tonomura's 1989 experiment filmed.
Placing a detector to see which slit each particle takes erases the interference, leaving two particle-like bands.

whyItMatters: The double-slit experiment is one of the most important and revealing demonstrations in all of physics, capturing the strangeness of quantum mechanics in a single striking image. In its original form it settled a long debate by showing that light behaves as a wave, but its quantum form goes far deeper: by revealing that individual particles build up an interference pattern as though each passed through both slits, yet register as single dots and lose their wave behavior when observed, it dramatizes wave-particle duality, the probabilistic wavefunction, and the central role of measurement in quantum theory. Richard Feynman held that the experiment contains the only mystery of quantum mechanics, and it remains the standard illustration of complementarity and the measurement problem, framing debates over how to interpret the theory. Readers of Physics World voted the single-electron version the most beautiful experiment in physics. As the clearest window into how nature behaves at the smallest scales, defying classical intuition, the double-slit experiment is fundamental to understanding quantum physics and endures as its defining puzzle.

working.text: direct particles or waves at a barrier with two narrow, closely spaced openings.
let each particle land as a single dot, and over many particles watch an interference pattern emerge.
add a detector that reveals which slit each particle took, and see the interference pattern vanish.

limits: The double-slit experiment is a demonstration whose interpretation, not its results, is what remains debated, since the mathematics of quantum mechanics predicts the outcomes precisely while different interpretations disagree about what they mean. The historical detail deserves care: it is disputed whether Thomas Young performed a literal two-slit experiment as popularly pictured, since his actual demonstrations used sunlight, pinholes, and narrow cards, so the tidy apparatus is partly a later idealization, and his interference work is best dated to his Bakerian Lectures around 1801 and 1803. A crucial misconception must be avoided: the loss of interference on measurement is a physical effect of the apparatus interacting with the particle and making which-path information available, not a result of a conscious mind observing. So the double-slit experiment robustly reveals wave-particle duality and the role of measurement, understood as an empirically settled but interpretively contested phenomenon whose popular tellings can overstate both Young's apparatus and the role of consciousness.
misreadings: The double-slit experiment does not show that consciousness collapses the wavefunction; the interference is lost because a physical detector interacts with the particle and records which-path information, whether or not anyone reads it. It does not mean the particle literally splits in two, but that its wavefunction, a probability amplitude, passes through both slits and interferes with itself. And Young's original was not necessarily the neat two-slit apparatus of textbooks, since his demonstrations used pinholes and cards, so treating measurement as requiring a mind, the particle as physically divided, or the popular history as exact, misreads a precisely predicted but interpretively deep experiment.
origin: An optics experiment associated with Thomas Young around 1801 to 1803, showing light interferes as a wave, later transformed into the defining demonstration of quantum wave-particle duality with single particles.
